articles.title: Monsoon-driven wildfires may have shaped human evolution
articles.summary: A reconstruction of East Africa's environment 1.75 million years ago suggests wildfires spiked during wetter times, which may have influenced human evolution
articles.content:
Wildfires in East Africa may have played a key role in human evolution Byelikova_Oksana/Getty Images

Wet climatic spells didn’t quench wildfires in East Africa’s Turkana basin 1.75 million years ago. Instead, they fuelled them. That’s what chemical traces from ancient plants in the region seem to suggest, and this pattern could have shaped our hominin ancestors’ evolution, including the use of fire and tools.

Rich in hominin fossils and archaeological finds, the Turkana basin – sometimes dubbed the Cradle of Humankind – has long been considered important for understanding the lives of our early ancestors. These include Homo erectus, a species that appeared about 2 million years ago and that is regarded as one of our earliest recognisably human ancestors.

The first truly complex stone tools were found here, too, in layers dating back to around 1.76 million years ago. Compared with earlier tools, these “Acheulean” tools were more advanced, and included refined multi-purpose hand axes, useful for both butchery and plant processing. The Acheulean technology then persisted for the next 1.5 million years.

Advertisement

One idea is that ancient hominins evolved the greater cognitive flexibility required to produce Acheulean tools – and to begin controlling fire – in response to dramatic environmental swings and rapidly changing ecosystems. But although previous studies have found evidence in favour of this “variability selection hypothesis”, establishing exactly what kinds of shifting environmental conditions may have driven these cognitive and technological advances has proved challenging.

Acheulean tools were more complex than earlier stone tools Heritage Image Partnership Ltd /Alamy

Now, Rachel Lupien at Aarhus University, Denmark, and her team think they may have an answer. They analysed chemical signatures in sediments that formed in the Turkana basin over a 21,000-year period, roughly 1.75 million years ago. With the information, they could reconstruct rainfall, vegetation and wildfire patterns when the earliest Acheulean tools were in use.

“Because these three powerful climate and ecosystem indicators are all from the same sample, we could directly look at how their relationships vary through time with no guesswork,” says Lupien.

The chemical signatures came from ancient leaf waxes and plant combustion, revealing how the nature of the vegetation shifted from woody to grassy conditions, and how wildfire intensity changed across time.

They found that the landscape was predominantly forested with limited wildfires for the first 5000 years of the study interval. It then became far more variable for the next 5000 years, fluctuating between very dry grasslands with occasional wildfires, perhaps caused by lightning strikes, and wetter forested conditions with far fewer fires. But during the final, longer period of the study interval, something surprising happened: rainfall increased significantly to produce monsoon conditions – and the number of wildfires rose, too.

“We find that higher precipitation leads to more vegetation growth, which allows fires to burn because of the additional biomass,” explains Lupien. Meanwhile, more fires limited vegetation expansion, which created a feedback loop. “What we can say from our data is that if humans were taking advantage of fire in Turkana, it would have been during these… wet intervals when monsoons were magnified.”

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Our Human Story Sign up to newsletter

“Here we’re now beginning to see the definite evidence that bushfires were there in their world,” says John Gowlett at the University of Liverpool, UK, who wasn’t involved in the analysis. It wouldn’t be surprising if ancient hominins then experimented with using those fires to improve their access to resources, he says.

For instance, frequent natural fires would have increased hominin opportunities for ‘fire foraging’: gathering up animals or plants that had been killed and cooked in the flames. It would also have allowed hominins to experiment with taking burning branches from natural wildfires and feeding them to keep fires burning longer, so they could cook food for themselves.

“It is far easier to keep a fire going than it is to start one,” says Matt Grove, a study co-author at the University of Liverpool, UK. “In this way, hominins could have started to reap the benefits of fire long before they were able to create it.”

A study published this year presented evidence of this type of fire use between 1.07 million and 1.79 million years ago at South Africa’s Wonderwerk Cave. Tentative evidence of fire use in Turkana dates back to around 1.5 million years ago.

The appearance of Acheulean stone tools during this interval may be further evidence of behavioural changes linked to the extremely variable environments in which ancient hominins evolved. Rick Potts at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington DC, who pioneered the variability selection hypothesis in the 1990s, thinks a link is plausible.

“This is the first paper I’ve encountered to illustrate the emergence of the Acheulean as a response to ecological variability and the process of variability selection,” he says. “Episodic and intense natural fires offer a novel contribution.”

articles.personality_title: Ancient wildfires in East Africa may have helped early humans learn to use fire and tools
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – About 1.75 million years ago, early human ancestors lived in East Africa’s Turkana basin, a place rich in fossils and ancient tools. Scientists have long studied this area to understand how humans evolved, especially how they started using fire and making advanced stone tools.

**What happened** – Researchers from Aarhus University studied chemical signs in ancient soil from the Turkana basin. These signs showed how rainfall, plants, and wildfires changed over 21,000 years. They found that during wetter times, when monsoon rains increased, wildfires also became more common. This is because more rain helped plants grow, which then fed the fires.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it suggests that wildfires were part of the environment when early humans lived there. These fires might have helped our ancestors learn to use fire for cooking and other tasks. For example, they could have collected food from places burned by wildfires or kept natural fires going longer. This could explain how humans started controlling fire before they knew how to make it themselves.

**What's next step** – Scientists will likely study other ancient sites to see if wildfires played a similar role in human evolution elsewhere. They may also look for more evidence of early fire use and how it connects to tool-making. This could give us a clearer picture of how early humans adapted to changing environments.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Wildfires fueled by ancient monsoons in East Africa may have helped early humans develop fire use and advanced tools, shaping our evolution.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les incendies anciens en Afrique de l’Est ont peut-être aidé les premiers humains à utiliser le feu et les outils
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Il y a environ 1,75 million d’années, les premiers ancêtres humains vivaient dans le bassin du Turkana en Afrique de l’Est, un lieu riche en fossiles et outils anciens. Les scientifiques étudient depuis longtemps cette région pour comprendre comment les humains ont évolué, notamment comment ils ont commencé à utiliser le feu et à fabriquer des outils en pierre avancés.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’université d’Aarhus ont analysé des signes chimiques dans le sol ancien du bassin du Turkana. Ces signes ont montré comment la pluie, les plantes et les incendies ont changé pendant 21 000 ans. Ils ont découvert que pendant les périodes plus humides, quand les moussons augmentaient, les incendies étaient aussi plus fréquents. Cela s’explique par le fait que plus de pluie faisait pousser plus de plantes, qui alimentaient ensuite les feux.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle suggère que les incendies faisaient partie de l’environnement où vivaient les premiers humains. Ces feux ont peut-être aidé nos ancêtres à apprendre à utiliser le feu pour cuisiner et d’autres tâches. Par exemple, ils pouvaient ramasser de la nourriture dans des zones brûlées ou entretenir des feux naturels plus longtemps. Cela pourrait expliquer comment les humains ont commencé à contrôler le feu avant de savoir comment le créer eux-mêmes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont probablement étudier d’autres sites anciens pour voir si les incendies ont joué un rôle similaire dans l’évolution humaine ailleurs. Ils chercheront aussi plus de preuves de l’utilisation ancienne du feu et de son lien avec la fabrication d’outils. Cela pourrait nous donner une image plus claire de la façon dont les premiers humains se sont adaptés aux environnements changeants.

**Phrase clé** – Les incendies alimentés par les moussons anciennes en Afrique de l’Est ont peut-être aidé les premiers humains à développer l’utilisation du feu et des outils avancés, façonnant ainsi notre évolution.
articles.personality_title_es: Los incendios antiguos en África oriental pudieron ayudar a los primeros humanos a usar el fuego y herramientas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Hace unos 1,75 millones de años, los primeros antepasados humanos vivían en la cuenca del Turkana, en África oriental, un lugar con muchos fósiles y herramientas antiguas. Los científicos han estudiado esta zona para entender cómo evolucionaron los humanos, especialmente cómo empezaron a usar el fuego y a fabricar herramientas de piedra más avanzadas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Aarhus analizaron señales químicas en el suelo antiguo del Turkana. Estas señales mostraron cómo cambiaron las lluvias, las plantas y los incendios durante 21,000 años. Descubrieron que en épocas más húmedas, cuando aumentaban las lluvias monzónicas, también crecían los incendios. Esto se debe a que más lluvia hacía crecer más plantas, que luego alimentaban los fuegos.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque sugiere que los incendios formaban parte del entorno donde vivían los primeros humanos. Estos fuegos podrían haber ayudado a nuestros antepasados a aprender a usar el fuego para cocinar y otras tareas. Por ejemplo, podían recoger alimentos en zonas quemadas o mantener el fuego natural encendido por más tiempo. Esto podría explicar cómo los humanos empezaron a controlar el fuego antes de saber cómo encenderlo.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos probablemente estudiarán otros sitios antiguos para ver si los incendios tuvieron un papel similar en la evolución humana en otros lugares. También buscarán más pruebas del uso temprano del fuego y su conexión con la fabricación de herramientas. Esto podría dar una imagen más clara de cómo los primeros humanos se adaptaron a ambientes cambiantes.

**Frase clave** – Los incendios alimentados por antiguos monzones en África oriental pudieron ayudar a los primeros humanos a desarrollar el uso del fuego y herramientas avanzadas, moldeando nuestra evolución.

articles.title: Why do people ask so few questions in conversation?
articles.summary: We've perhaps been conditioned to not ask too many questions, in case it comes across as rude or prying. But columnist David Robson argues that asking people open-ended questions benefits our wellbeing, and doesn't have to be complicated
articles.content:
We've perhaps been conditioned to not ask too many questions, in case it comes across as rude or prying. But columnist David Robson argues that asking people open-ended questions benefits our wellbeing, and doesn't have to be complicated

Forget small talk about the weather, asking someone about their favourite childhood memory could lead to an insightful conversation Shutterstock/RossHelen

I was at a friend’s birthday party recently when I found myself sitting next to a writer I didn’t know. Oh good, I thought optimistically, we might be able to bond over the joys and pains of the job. Two hours later, I knew the ins and outs of the surrealist novel he was writing, but he found out very little about me, since he didn’t ask a single question in return.

I am sure this will be familiar to many readers, so I was delighted to come across some new work on “interpersonal curiosity” by Niobe Way, a professor of applied psychology at New York University. She suggests that, from a young age, Western patriarchal culture subtly discourages us from demonstrating an interest in others – an idea reinforced by masculine stereotypes. Fortunately, she has plenty of suggestions for ways to cultivate it in ourselves and our children.

Way tells me that she was inspired by her personal experience of moving to Shanghai for a few months with her young children in 2007. It was, she says, “a transformative experience”. When she returned to the US, however, she tried to talk to her friends about the amazing time that she’d had, with little success. “No one, literally nobody, asked me questions about it,” she says. “And I remember saying, what is going on with people’s curiosity?”

Advertisement

Nearly 20 years later, she is finally answering that question. Previous research on curiosity, she says, had mostly focused on intellectual interests in the physical, material and natural world, while largely neglecting to measure people’s inquisitiveness about others’ lives and its consequences.

As a developmental psychologist, Way has so far focused her efforts on children and adolescents. She and her colleagues asked 389 school students aged 11-13 to describe the two questions that they would most like to ask their closest friend, teacher and primary caregivers. They received a wide variety of responses. Some of the participants reported having no questions at all, while others opted for simple information-seeking (such as “When is dinner?” or “What is the point of this work?”). Those who wished to probe others’ personal lives and relationships, however, had better friendships and greater overall wellbeing.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

Such findings are perhaps unsurprising: supportive relationships are known to be central to our health and happiness, and asking others questions about their lives is surely one of the best ways to build those bonds. “It really is the secret sauce of all human connection,” says Way.

The big question, then, is why we don’t do it more often. Way suggests that we have been conditioned to think that it is rude to pry into others’ lives, and the rise of individualism means that we also simply care less about the people around us. In their study of adolescent students, however, Way and her colleagues found that boys were about twice as likely to report having “no questions” than girls – suggesting that gender roles may play a large part.

Earlier this year, Way published a paper that tackled this topic head-on. To measure their adherence to masculine stereotypes, each adolescent was asked to rate their agreement with statements such as “I do not let it show to my friends when my feelings are hurt” and “It is necessary for me to fight others in order to gain respect.” As hypothesised, the team found that these scores were inversely correlated with interpersonal curiosity, meaning that the more someone endorsed macho values, the less likely they were to say they enjoyed hearing others’ stories. And this, in turn, seemed to have a big influence on the quality of their friendships, measured by things like the amount of free time they spent with their closest friend and the amount of social support they received from them.

You may imagine that this affected only the boys – and the connection was indeed much stronger for those who identified as male. Although some girls have started to associate the tough-guy image with success, and internalised the associated behaviour, this didn’t seem to be so closely linked to interpersonal curiosity, which independently predicted their relationship quality.

Sexist assumptions about interpersonal curiosity may even explain why it has been understudied in science. “We think that interpersonal curiosity is feminine, and we don’t value what we’ve deemed feminine,” says Way, whose book Rebels with a Cause: Reimagining boys, ourselves and our culture explores these themes. “But this ‘soft’ side is essential for our social species.”

Can we ever overcome this cultural conditioning? Way argues that children are born to be interpersonally curious, and that innate interest can be reawakened with the right education. To do so, she designed the Listening with Curiosity Project, a 26-lesson curriculum for adolescent students in New York Public Schools. It includes advice on asking open-ended questions and techniques to encourage people to open up about their experiences with greater nuance and detail – with plenty of opportunity for practice. The early evidence suggests it works: by the end of the curriculum, the students showed greater curiosity and increased friendship quality, with boys showing the biggest gains.

Way thinks that plenty of adults could also benefit from a bit of practice. You might start out with someone you know, by asking them about their favourite childhood memory, a topic that most people enjoy discussing. You can then use this opportunity to show your genuine interest in what they say through lots of follow-up questions.

You could even try it at a party, she suggests. Simply explain that you’ve been reading about the benefits of asking deep questions, then pick a topic to begin with.

You may feel shy about getting started, but Way reassures me that it will be far more rewarding than you expect. When she encourages her students to try the exercise, they almost all take pleasure in the experience. “We are starving to be asked real questions,” she says. “Just do it.”

David Robson’s latest book is The Laws of Connection: 13 social strategies that will transform your life. If you have a question that you would like answered in his column, please send him a message at davidrobson.me/contact

articles.personality_title: Asking questions helps build better friendships and wellbeing
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people avoid asking questions in conversations because they worry it might seem rude or too personal. A new study shows that asking open-ended questions can actually improve our relationships and happiness.

**What happened** – Professor Niobe Way from New York University studied how curious young people are about others. She found that children and teenagers who ask deep questions about their friends’ and family’s lives tend to have better friendships and feel happier. She also created a school program that teaches students how to ask these questions, and it helped improve their social connections.

**Impact** – This research is important because it shows that being curious about others is good for our mental health and friendships. It also explains that cultural ideas, like “boys shouldn’t show feelings,” make some people less likely to ask questions, which can hurt their relationships. The school program helped students practice curiosity, especially boys, and made their friendships stronger.

**What's next step** – The next step is to encourage more schools and adults to try teaching and practicing asking open-ended questions. This could help many people build closer friendships and feel more connected. Starting with simple questions, like asking about someone’s favorite childhood memory, is a good way to begin.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Learning to ask curious, open questions helps people form stronger friendships and improves their wellbeing.
articles.personality_title_fr: Poser des questions renforce les amitiés et le bien-être
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup de gens évitent de poser des questions en conversation par peur d’être impolis ou trop intrusifs. Une nouvelle étude montre que poser des questions ouvertes peut en fait améliorer nos relations et notre bonheur.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La professeure Niobe Way, de l’Université de New York, a étudié la curiosité des jeunes envers les autres. Elle a découvert que les enfants et adolescents qui posent des questions profondes sur la vie de leurs amis et famille ont de meilleures amitiés et se sentent plus heureux. Elle a aussi créé un programme scolaire pour apprendre à poser ces questions, ce qui a renforcé leurs liens sociaux.

**Impact** – Cette recherche est importante car elle montre que s’intéresser aux autres est bon pour la santé mentale et les amitiés. Elle explique aussi que des idées culturelles, comme « les garçons ne montrent pas leurs émotions », empêchent certains de poser des questions, ce qui nuit à leurs relations. Le programme scolaire a aidé les élèves, surtout les garçons, à pratiquer la curiosité et à améliorer leurs amitiés.

**Prochaine étape** – L’étape suivante est d’inciter plus d’écoles et d’adultes à enseigner et pratiquer la pose de questions ouvertes. Cela pourrait aider beaucoup de personnes à créer des liens plus forts et à se sentir plus connectées. Commencer par des questions simples, comme demander un souvenir d’enfance préféré, est un bon début.

**Phrase clé** – Apprendre à poser des questions ouvertes et curieuses aide à créer des amitiés plus fortes et améliore le bien-être.
articles.personality_title_es: Hacer preguntas fortalece amistades y bienestar
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas evitan hacer preguntas en las conversaciones por miedo a parecer groseros o demasiado curiosos. Un nuevo estudio muestra que hacer preguntas abiertas puede mejorar nuestras relaciones y felicidad.

**Qué pasó** – La profesora Niobe Way, de la Universidad de Nueva York, estudió la curiosidad interpersonal en jóvenes. Descubrió que niños y adolescentes que hacen preguntas profundas sobre la vida de sus amigos y familiares tienen mejores amistades y se sienten más felices. También creó un programa escolar para enseñar a hacer estas preguntas, lo que mejoró sus conexiones sociales.

**Impacto** – Esta investigación es importante porque muestra que interesarse por los demás es bueno para la salud mental y las amistades. También explica que ideas culturales, como “los niños no deben mostrar sentimientos”, hacen que algunos eviten preguntar, lo que afecta sus relaciones. El programa ayudó especialmente a los niños a practicar la curiosidad y fortalecer sus amistades.

**Próximo paso** – El siguiente paso es animar a más escuelas y adultos a enseñar y practicar hacer preguntas abiertas. Esto podría ayudar a muchas personas a crear lazos más fuertes y sentirse más conectados. Empezar con preguntas simples, como preguntar por un recuerdo favorito de la infancia, es una buena forma.

**Frase clave** – Aprender a hacer preguntas abiertas y curiosas ayuda a formar amistades más fuertes y mejora el bienestar.
